title: Predicting Market Trends: The Engineering Behind a Housing Price ML Model
excerpt: Building a machine learning model for real estate prices is more than just picking an algorithm. It's about data wrangling, feature engineering, and turning a model into a usable product.

content.text: When I decided to build a machine learning model for predicting house prices in Chennai, I quickly realized that the real challenge wasn't the algorithm — it was everything around it. Data cleaning, feature engineering, and turning a notebook experiment into a reliable service are where most of the work happens.

Real estate data is messy. I had to aggregate listings from various sources, handle missing values, and standardize location data. For a city like Chennai with diverse neighborhoods, encoding location was crucial. I used one-hot encoding for zones and created distance-based features to key landmarks and transit hubs.
Feature Engineering: Where Domain Knowledge Matters

Beyond raw features, I engineered new ones: age of the property, proximity to schools and hospitals, and even a 'liquor store density' feature inspired by a classic real estate heuristic. The goal was to capture nuances that a linear model could interpret.

For a use case like price prediction, Linear Regression offered the perfect balance of interpretability and performance. Stakeholders needed to understand what drove prices, not just a black-box prediction. I trained on a split of historical data, and while the RMSE was acceptable, the R-squared revealed the limitations of a purely linear approach in a non-linear market.
The simplest model that explains the data is often the most trustworthy in production.
content.author: Roshan Lal Yogi

content.text: I wrapped the model in a FastAPI endpoint, using joblib for serialization. The endpoint accepted features and returned a price range. On the Flutter side, I built a simple form to collect inputs. The gap between a Jupyter notebook and a production API is vast: error handling, input validation, and logging became top priorities.

Building this model taught me that AI projects are software engineering projects first. The model is just one component. The pipeline, the API, the client integration — these are what make the AI useful. For anyone stepping into ML, start with a simple model, ship it early, and focus on the engineering around it.
